Living Well / Proposed experiment

Proposed experiment: a notebook or AI for a weekly reflection?

Proposed experiment · 3 min read · Published October 8, 2026

On this page
  1. State the question before trying either method
  2. Use ordinary occasions and record the order
  3. Keep the AI contribution bounded
  4. Observe usefulness after the reflection
  5. Report the limits with the result
  6. One question to take with you

The question is not which method produces the most polished reflection. It is which one helps you notice something useful and take an appropriate next step with less unnecessary work.

Status: proposed experiment. This is a ready-to-try plan, not a completed trial, personal result, or claim of effectiveness. No findings are being reported.

State the question before trying either method

This is a proposed personal comparison, not a completed study. Choose a low-stakes weekly reflection you are comfortable doing in either format. Write what you expect each method to offer and what would count against your preferred option.

Keep the task modest and comparable. You might use the same questions about a useful moment, an unresolved task, and one next action. Do not include intimate material merely to give the AI more context. The paper version can remain completely private.

Use ordinary occasions and record the order

Try the notebook and the AI-assisted approach on separate comparable occasions. Record which came first, how much time you spent, and anything unusual about the week. An especially busy or enjoyable week may explain more than the method.

Repeating or alternating the order can help you notice an obvious order effect, but it does not turn the exercise into a controlled trial. Familiarity with one method, changing circumstances, and your expectations remain possible influences.

Keep the AI contribution bounded

Use a de-identified description and ask for questions or a clearer structure, not a diagnosis, spiritual interpretation, or statement of your true priorities. Save only what you need in a place you control. Check the service's current data practices before sharing information.

Count the time spent preparing the prompt, reviewing the response, removing wrong assumptions, and transferring any useful result. A system that writes quickly may still create more total work than a notebook.

Observe usefulness after the reflection

Record whether you identified something specific, whether the next action made sense, and whether you actually used the result. Note discomfort, pressure to overexplain, or dependence on repeated reassurance as reasons to change or stop the exercise.

Do not interpret a longer entry or more encouraging language as evidence of greater insight. Include what did not help. No-AI, occasional AI, and abandoning formal weekly reflection are all acceptable outcomes.

Report the limits with the result

Use the blank field-note worksheet. A future report should include what was actually done, departures from the plan, effort, observations, other possible explanations, and the decision to keep or stop.

The result could inform your own next attempt. It would not establish that one method improves wellbeing, is better for all readers, or caused every difference you noticed. Until someone actually completes and reports this comparison, there are no findings to cite.

One optional practice

Write the question and stopping rule before the first attempt. Keep essential responsibilities and privacy intact. You can stop at any point without owing the experiment a completed result.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

Which method leaves you more able to return to life rather than continue analyzing it?
